mcqs.question: Why is the 'no two conflicting directions are ever green' invariant risky to enforce only informally, by a developer manually checking each phase?
options: It isn't risky — traffic engineers always verify this by hand before deployment
The invariant only matters during emergency-vehicle preemption, not the normal cycle
A future change to the phase table (a new phase, a tweaked duration) can silently violate the invariant unless the code itself checks every proposed transition against a conflict rule
Informal enforcement is fine because all-red clearance already guarantees safety on its own
mcqs.explanation: Manual review doesn't scale to future edits made by someone unaware of every existing combination — the invariant has to be checked in code on every transition. It applies to the normal cycle just as much as preemption, and all-red clearance only helps if it's actually reached, which is exactly what an unchecked transition could skip.

mcqs.question: In the ConflictMatrix design, why is isSafe() checked on every transition, including ones triggered by emergency preemption?
options: Because preemption requests are less reliable than the timer
Because there is no code path that's allowed to apply a Phase without passing the same safety check — a special-cased exception for preemption would reopen exactly the risk the check exists to close
It isn't necessary for preemption, since emergency vehicles have the right of way regardless
Because the conflict matrix is only valid during daytime operation
mcqs.explanation: The safety guarantee only holds if every transition, with no exceptions, goes through the same check — carving out preemption as a special case reintroduces the exact bug the matrix is meant to prevent. Right-of-way for emergency vehicles doesn't override physics; two green conflicting directions are still a collision. Reliability of the request source and time of day are irrelevant to the check itself.

mcqs.question: Why does Controller.tick() run on a fixed schedule and check elapsed time, rather than having hardware directly trigger phase transitions?
options: It keeps a single, predictable place — the tick loop — where all transition logic, including the safety check, runs, instead of being triggered from multiple uncoordinated hardware signals
It's slower, but required by traffic law
Hardware timers cannot be trusted to measure time accurately
It removes the need for a Phase class entirely
mcqs.explanation: Centralizing transitions in one polled loop means there's exactly one code path that can change the active phase, which is what makes a single safety check sufficient. There's no such legal requirement, hardware timers are generally reliable, and Phase is still needed either way.

mcqs.question: For an agency operating many different intersection shapes (four-way, T-junction, protected-turn), why does a data-driven phase table scale better than a hardcoded sequence in Controller?
options: Data-driven tables are always faster to execute at runtime than hardcoded logic
Hardcoded sequences cannot support pedestrian crossings
Data-driven tables remove the need for a ConflictMatrix
New or different intersection layouts become a new table read at startup instead of a code change to the class that also enforces safety, narrowing what needs review for correctness
mcqs.explanation: The real win is isolating change: a new intersection shape becomes a config file, not an edit to the safety-critical Controller class. Runtime speed isn't meaningfully different, pedestrian crossings work fine with either approach, and ConflictMatrix is still needed regardless of where the phase table lives.

mcqs.question: Why should all-red clearance be modeled as its own first-class Phase rather than an informal pause inserted between the main phases?
options: Because pauses are not permitted under most traffic-control hardware standards

As a first-class Phase, it goes through the same ConflictMatrix check and phase-table entry as any other phase, so it can't be silently skipped by a rushed edit or an interrupt jumping straight between conflicting greens
Because it makes the timer's tick() implementation run faster
Because pedestrian crossings only work during all-red clearance
mcqs.explanation: Treating clearance as a real Phase means it's subject to the exact same safety machinery as every other phase, so it can't be quietly bypassed. It has nothing to do with hardware standards, tick() performance, or pedestrian crossings specifically.
